content.p: In the last week of November 1941, trains that had left Germany and Austria for Riga were sent to Kaunas in Lithuania instead. At least some of the people on board had been told they were being sent to work in the east. Within a few days of arriving they were taken to the Ninth Fort, a Tsarist-era fortress on the edge of the city, and shot into pits that had been dug weeks earlier. By the count of the unit that did the shooting, 2,934 people died on 25 November and 2,000 more on 29 November.

The historian Wolfgang Scheffler, in a lecture published by the German war graves commission, called these executions the first mass shootings of German Jews. The killers belonged to Einsatzkommando 3, a unit commanded by Karl Jäger, which worked with German Order Police and Lithuanian auxiliaries. The headline figures come from Jäger's own report, whose precision a later historian has questioned.
content.h2: A fort with a history of its own
content.p: The Ninth Fort was one of a ring of fortifications built around Kaunas for the Russian Empire. The museum that now occupies the site says construction began in 1903 and that German troops took the fortress in 1915. Between the wars independent Lithuania used the fort as a division of its hard-labour prison, and from 1930 it held political prisoners. After the Soviet occupation of June 1940 it became a transit point for people being sent to the Gulag.

When Germany occupied Lithuania at the end of June 1941, the fort took on a darker role. The museum states that about 50,000 people were murdered there over three years, around 30,000 of them Jews, together with Lithuanians, Poles, Russians and others. Aya Ben-Naftali of the Massuah Institute, writing in a paper published by YIVO, argues that the fort was chosen as the main execution site in advance, apparently mainly because it lay close to the Vilijampole suburb where the Kaunas ghetto was set up.

The pits came first. Ben-Naftali reports that fourteen of them were dug on a terrace about 150 metres west of the fort walls, starting in the second half of July 1941 and finishing about three months later. About 1,000 Soviet prisoners of war did the digging, most of them dying of disease or starvation, and those still alive in late October were killed. She reads the pits' capacity, room for more than 40,000 bodies, as a sign that the Security Police had planned to kill all of the roughly 30,000 Jews of Kaunas. The pits were in use by early October: Jäger's report records 1,845 people shot at the fort on 4 October and 9,200 from the ghetto on 29 October. The November killings came a month later.
content.h2: Why the trains went to Kaunas
content.p: Scheffler explains that Hitler approved the deportation of Jews from the Reich only in September 1941, at first in limited numbers. The city council of Lodz resisted taking 60,000 and the number was cut to 20,000. Minsk and Riga were then chosen as destinations for 50,000 people, but the Minsk transports were called off after army protests, with winter setting in and defeat looming outside Moscow. Riga had no space either, despite assurances from Franz Stahlecker, the commander of Einsatzgruppe A. The Higher SS and Police Leader for the region, Friedrich Jeckeln, ordered the Riga ghetto cleared; on 30 November and again on 8 and 9 December, 26,500 Latvian Jews were murdered in the Rumbula woods.

Because these measures came late, Scheffler writes, the first five transports meant for Riga were sent to Kaunas after several delays. Why they were diverted is not explained in the pages consulted. Ben-Naftali adds that the Security Police and SD in Lithuania treated the killing of Reich Jews at the fort as an extension of existing instructions to destroy Jews in the occupied areas.
The trains left at different times, and local memorial work has recovered what happened to each.

Berlin. The community magazine Jüdisches Berlin reports that people were taken from their homes and held in a synagogue that served as the city's assembly point for deportations. On the night of 17 November they were marched through the western part of the city to Grunewald station, where a passenger train waited. It was the sixth deportation from Berlin, and it arrived at Kaunas on 21 November. The magazine adds that nothing is known of what the victims lived through in their last four days.

Munich. The first transport from Munich left on 20 November from the barracks camp in Milbertshofen. The Jewish Museum Munich's installation gives 998 deportees, 978 of them from Munich itself, who had been told they would be put to work. The biography of Jenny Kissinger, published by the Munich Erinnerungszeichen project, says the people were kept for three days in the cellar of Fort IX and shot there on 25 November. Jenny Kissinger, a teacher's wife and mother of two boys, was among them with her family.

Frankfurt. The train left Frankfurt am Main on 22 November. The Neu-Isenburg memorial book says it was the third transport from the city and that it probably reached Kaunas on 24 November. Among the passengers was Denny Löwenstein, born in September 1939, who was two years old when he was shot. The Jüdische Allgemeine puts the number of Frankfurt deportees at 992 and says all were shot three days after leaving.

Vienna and Breslau. Jäger's report names these two cities for the second massacre, on 29 November, and Scheffler's lecture gives the same pairing. The pages consulted do not describe the journeys of these two transports.

Jäger's report, dated 1 December 1941, records both killings. For 25 November it lists 1,159 men, 1,600 women and 175 children, "resettlers from Berlin, Munich and Frankfurt am Main", a total of 2,934. For 29 November it lists 693 men, 1,155 women and 152 children, resettlers from Vienna and Breslau, a total of 2,000. The report uses the word "Jews" for men and "Jewesses" for women, and the totals above are its own. Scheffler's lecture gives 893 men for the second day, which does not add up to the stated total, so 693 appears to be the correct figure. A separate line in the report for 29 November records another 34 people at the same place: 17 Jewish men, one Jewish woman convicted under the ghetto rules, a German citizen who had converted to the Jewish faith and attended rabbinical school, and fifteen men it calls terrorists from the "Kalinin group". Those 34 were not deportees from the Reich.

The Jüdische Allgemeine reports that every one of the Frankfurt deportees was shot. The Jewish Museum Munich says the Munich, Berlin and Frankfurt deportees were shot together at the fort's moats, by Einsatzkommando 3 under Jäger. A Berlin district memorial page for a woman deported on 17 November says the victims were killed by Einsatzkommando 3 together with German and Lithuanian auxiliary police.

Ben-Naftali describes how the machinery worked at the fort during the autumn. Jäger took personal command of the killing there, helped by two Gestapo officers. Dozens of Security Police and Einsatzkommando men were assisted by hundreds of Lithuanian auxiliary policemen and by a permanent Lithuanian garrison, with a volunteer firing party drawn from the police battalions. The victims, she says, were not registered by name, and each operation worked to a quota. Her account relies largely on testimony from perpetrators and from prisoners who later buried the dead. Her paper concentrates on the ghetto actions of September and October; for the November shootings, the Berlin district page above names Lithuanian auxiliary police as taking part.

Ben-Naftali questions the report's exactness. Lithuanian witnesses said no written orders were issued at the site and no accurate count was kept; the totals were set by quotas. Jäger's figures are nevertheless precise, and she suggests he took them from where victims were assembled. She names three possible inputs: reports by the Jewish police commander, lists drawn up by the ghetto council, and lists of deportations from the Reich that the Reich Security Main Office sent him. For the November transports the last of these is plausible, since the trains came from outside Lithuania, though she does not say which source he used for them.

Local counts do not match each other or the report exactly. Berlin's memorial plaque names 1,006 murdered Berlin residents. The Munich exhibit gives 998 deportees from a single transport. Frankfurt's figure is 992. Jäger's 25 November total of 2,934 divides into three cities by sex and age, not by origin, so it cannot be set against those figures line by line.

Scheffler notes that the first transport to reach Riga directly, about 730 Berlin Jews who left Berlin on 27 November, was killed on the morning of 30 November, just before the Latvian Jews were taken to Rumbula. Transports that arrived in the first days of December were sent to the Jungfernhof camp near the city.

In Lithuania, Jäger declared his task complete. His report states: "Today I can confirm that our objective, to solve the Jewish problem for Lithuania, has been achieved by EK 3." He wrote that the Jewish workers still alive were needed urgently and would be needed more after the winter. The report gives the total of its unit's executions as 137,346 people, including 4,000 killed in pogroms and executions before the unit took over. Ben-Naftali notes that in December 1941 the Reichskommissar for the Ostland, Heinrich Lohse, ordered a pause in killing skilled Jewish workers. That halted the large operations at the fort, but individual and small-group executions continued there until the occupation ended.

The museum says the fort's other victims included Jews from Austria, France and Czechoslovakia, most of the foreigners being killed in November and December 1941 and the last large French group in May 1944. In the second half of 1943 the Germans tried to destroy the evidence by exhuming and burning the bodies. On 25 December 1943 a group of 64 prisoners from the burning team escaped. The Baltic Times, citing the museum's guides, says 37 were later recaptured and killed and 27 reached freedom.
content.h2: The man who wrote the report
content.p: Karl Jäger was born in 1888, joined the Nazi party in 1923 and became an SS-Standartenführer in the Security Service in 1938, according to the newspaper junge Welt. After the war, it says, he lived under his real name near Heidelberg as a farm labourer. He was arrested in 1959 and killed himself in prison. The paper adds that his home town of Waldkirch long avoided the subject, and that its council later decided to put up a memorial to the Jewish population murdered in Lithuania.

On the seventieth anniversary, 25 November 2011, a plaque for the 1,006 murdered Berlin residents was unveiled at the fort. It was funded jointly by the mayor of Berlin, the Centrum Judaicum foundation and the foundation for the memorial to the murdered Jews of Europe. Lithuanian survivors attended, and Hermann Simon spoke for the Jewish community. He named some of the dead, among them seven-year-old Rosa Rita Zaduk and six-year-old Sally Jacobsberg, and said that remembering victims meant not forgetting the perpetrators.

In 2018 the Jüdische Allgemeine reported the dedication of a stone for the 992 Frankfurt deportees, paid for in the name of Frankfurt and 36 other towns and cities. It adds to the markers already placed by Berlin and Munich. The project was led by the Brüder-Schönfeld-Forum of Maintal, named for two brothers, aged ten and eleven in 1941, who were killed in the shootings with their parents.
